newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wheat growers angered, frustrated by CWB move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat growers angered, frustrated by CWB move.

text.p: U.S. wheat growers reacted with anger and frustration on Wednesday after the Canadian Wheat Board said it would export wheat through the U.S. Pacific Northwest because of severe grain transportation delays in Canada.

"Now they're using our tracks, our ports, our trains and tying up our delivery system for theirs, and they're stealing our market besides. It's starting to hurt," said Tim Dufault, a spokesman for the Minnesota Association of Wheat Growers.

A CWB spokeswoman told Reuters Wednesday that the state wheat board had sent an "average-sized" cargo of wheat to load in Portland. She said Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp was railing the grain from Winnipeg.
Growers said it was ironic that the CWB had undercut U.S. prices with subsidies, only then to rely on U.S. facilities when the transport system faltered.

"We think it's a just reward that they can't get their fire sale wheat shipped, and of course now they're using the U.S. system to alleviate that problem," said Ross Fitzgerald, a spokesman for the Montana Grain Growers Association.
Weather and transportation problems have slowed shipment of wheat to Canadian ports over the past several weeks. On Tuesday, 39 ships waited to load grains and oilseeds on Canada's Pacific Coast.
In Washington, a spokesman for U.S. Sen. Byron Dorgan of North Dakota said the shipment was an example of "the unfair situation that exists" in the global wheat trade.

He also questioned how the Canadians could justify shipping wheat through the United States, while only last year they used what he called "phony concerns" about karnal bunt fungus to restrict U.S. wheat shipments on the Great Lakes.
U.S. growers took the occasion to blast what they perceived as unfair trading practices by the monopolistic CWB.

"They're undercutting (U.S. wheat prices) all the time because they say they've got a better system, and the minute their system hits a snag they come through the U.S. to add insult to injury," Dufault said.

But not all U.S. reaction was negative. Jonathan Schlueter, executive vice president of Pacific Northwest Grain and Feed Association, Inc, suggested U.S. shippers would likely welcome the added business.

"The Northwest has surplus capacity. The business in wheat in this region... is down 18 to 20 percent this year. Corn's probably (down) between 20 and 25 percent," Schlueter said, noting that the shipping deal made economic sense for both sides.
"These companies and facilities are in business to stay in business. If there's surplus capacity and there's a paying customer, it makes sense to do the business," her said.
